title: A Novel Deep Learning-Based Data Analysis Model for Solar Photovoltaic Power Generation and Electrical Consumption Forecasting in the Smart Power Grid
text:
Title: A Novel Deep Learning-Based Data Analysis Model for Solar Photovoltaic Power Generation and Electrical Consumption Forecasting in the Smart Power Grid
Authors: Mbey, Yem Souhe, Foba Kakeu & Teplaira Boum (2024)
Journal / Source: Applied Computational Intelligence and Soft Computing, Vol. 2024, Article 9257508 (Hindawi), DOI: 10.1155/2024/9257508
Objective: To review individual and hybrid deep-learning methods used for smart-grid PV generation and electricity-consumption forecasting, and to propose a novel hybrid MLP-LSTM-GA model performing both long-term electrical-consumption forecasting and short-term PV power-generation forecasting using climate and socioeconomic data.
Methodology: Five models implemented and compared: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP, 2000 neurons), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM, 200 hidden units), Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS), and a novel hybrid MLP-LSTM-GA model (MLP performs feature extraction/preprocessing, feeding into an LSTM for temporal prediction; a Genetic Algorithm tunes bias σ, weight ω, cost error C and transfer function φ, using a quadratic radial basis transfer function). Training time 300s, validation time 60s. Implemented in MATLAB R2020b.
Key Findings: MLP alone deviates from actual data during 2011–2020 due to slow convergence; LSTM tracks actual consumption closely, especially 2015–2020; SVM diverges over time; ANFIS outperforms SVM but fluctuates. Combining MLP (feature extraction) with LSTM (temporal learning) and GA optimisation substantially reduces error versus any single model. Predicted Cameroon consumption could reach ~1508 GWh by 2030. First study to jointly forecast long-term consumption and short-term PV generation within the same hybrid framework.
Limitations / Gaps: PV forecasting accuracy is highly dependent on uncertain/variable climate conditions; dataset limited to a single city (Douala) and single country (generalizability concerns); excludes atmospheric pressure, precipitation, cloud cover/nebulosity, or sky-image data (sensor unavailability); relies on historical trend-based socio-economic projections that may not hold under structural economic shocks.
Future Work: Incorporate additional climatic factors (atmospheric pressure, precipitation, nebulosity, sky imagery); integrate IoT-based real-time sensor data; extend the hybrid model to other smart-grid applications (e.g., fault detection) and other geographic regions.

title: Using Machine Learning Algorithms to Forecast Solar Energy Power Output
text:
Title: Using Machine Learning Algorithms to Forecast Solar Energy Power Output
Authors: Lari, Sanfilippo, Bachour & Perez-Astudillo (2025)
Journal / Source: Electronics, 14(5), 866, MDPI, DOI: 10.3390/electronics14050866
Objective: To evaluate and compare four supervised machine-learning algorithms (Linear Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost) for forecasting Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI)/solar PV power output across multiple forecast horizons, and to assess how forecast-window length affects prediction accuracy.
Methodology: Four supervised ML algorithms compared: Linear Regression, Decision Tree (Gini/entropy/information-gain splitting), Random Forest (ensemble of decision trees with randomised construction to curb overfitting), and XGBoost (gradient-boosted trees). Implemented in Python using Scikit-Learn. Evaluated separately at five forecast horizons (0.5, 3, 6, 12, 24 h).
Key Findings: Forecast accuracy generally degrades as the horizon lengthens because GHI is highly sensitive to fast-changing weather; Linear Regression instead showed an irregular/sine-shaped error profile. Decision Tree and Random Forest exhibited sigmoid-shaped MAE/RMSE curves peaking around the 12-h window; XGBoost's RMSE grew near-exponentially with horizon length. Ensemble/tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost) consistently outperformed simpler linear/single-tree models by better capturing non-linear, weather-driven patterns and handling missing data more robustly. The 6-h window offered the best overall forecast reliability for the tree-based/ensemble models.
Limitations / Gaps: Limited to a single geographic location (Doha, Qatar) and a single (arid/desert) climate type, restricting generalizability; restricted to four 'classic' supervised ML algorithms — no deep-learning (LSTM/CNN) comparison; only solar radiation used as the predictive driver — other meteorological variables (cloud cover, humidity, wind) not modeled as separate features; relatively coarse mean-imputation strategy for missing data; requires substantial historical data, which may not exist for all target regions.
Future Work: Extend the comparison to deep-learning models (LSTM, CNN, hybrid architectures); test across multiple climates/geographies; incorporate additional meteorological covariates; develop software packages for site-specific PV plant design using the validated ML pipeline.

title: Residential Solar Adoption — Main Determinants and the Future of Small-Scale Photovoltaics
text:
Title: Residential Solar Adoption — Main Determinants and the Future of Small-Scale Photovoltaics
Authors: Reissl, Sarmiento & Emmerling (2025)
Journal / Source: Environmental Research: Energy, 2, 035002, IOP Publishing, DOI: 10.1088/2753-3751/ade79a
Objective: To develop and calibrate a data-driven agent-based microsimulation model of household residential PV-adoption decisions in Germany, replicate historical adoption (2007–2020), and project future adoption scenarios (to 2050) incorporating economic profitability, financial constraints, environmental attitudes, and peer effects, differentiated by income decile, dwelling type and urban/rural location.
Methodology: Data-driven agent-based / heterogeneous-household microsimulation model (not a supervised ML forecasting model). Each household makes a binary annual PV-adoption decision based on an expected-utility framework combining (i) discounted expected profitability (electricity savings + feed-in-tariff revenue minus loan interest, individual discount rates calibrated to Newell & Siikamäki 2015), (ii) environmental attitude ('green glow'), and (iii) peer effects (Bass-diffusion-style social contagion based on same-income-decile/same-area PV-ownership share). A stylised banking sector models credit rationing via a debt-service-to-income cap. Seven free parameters (α, β, γ1, γ2, γ3, δ, ξ) calibrated via Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO; 4 swarms × 30 particles × 250 combinations = 30,000 combinations, each averaged over 108 seeded runs) minimising sum-of-squared error against empirical adoption time series. Baseline, 'high-PV' and 'low-PV' policy scenarios simulated to 2050; five additional sensitivity analyses (curtailment, geographic capacity-factor variation, panel orientation, installation restrictions).
Key Findings: Adoption follows a classic sigmoid diffusion-of-innovation curve driven by peer effects and declining technology costs. Strong, persistent income-based disparities: the highest income decile reaches ~76.6–77% adoption by 2050 vs only ~6–6.1% for the lowest decile — reflecting a regressive distribution of feed-in-tariff subsidies (wealthier/rural households capture disproportionately larger FIT payments, e.g. >€500M to the richest urban decile vs <€100M to the poorest rural decile by 2023). Policy levers (technology-cost decline rate, electricity-price growth, feed-in-tariff duration/level) are critical determinants of both the speed and equity of adoption. Extensive sensitivity analysis (curtailment, capacity factor, orientation, installation restrictions) confirms the income-adoption gap is robust (high-income >75%, low-income <10% in all scenarios) even though headline adoption rates vary by only 2–4 percentage points. Cumulative feed-in-tariff payments could reach ~200 billion EUR by mid-century in the baseline scenario.
Limitations / Gaps: Does not incorporate sophisticated/rational household expectation formation — agents lack foresight on future price or policy changes; feed-in tariffs and other policy variables treated as exogenous and certain (ignoring policy-credibility/uncertainty effects); excludes complementary/coupled technologies (home battery storage, EVs, heat pumps) that could alter PV-adoption incentives; abstracts from grid-level physical constraints (interconnection capacity, curtailment, rate-structure reforms) that could bind well before the ~47% saturation level — authors note projections should be read as upper bounds; single-country (Germany) case study limiting generalizability.
Future Work: Extend the model to include coupled adoption of home battery storage, electric vehicles and heat pumps; model alternative policy frameworks (e.g., self-consumption/net-metering incentives instead of feed-in tariffs); integrate with power-grid stability/curtailment models; apply the modelling framework comparatively to other countries/regions to generalise policy insights; explore dynamic/declining income-adoption disparities over time as technology matures.

title: Machine Learning Reduces Soft Costs for Residential Solar Photovoltaics
text:
Title: Machine Learning Reduces Soft Costs for Residential Solar Photovoltaics
Authors: Dong, Nemet, Gao, Barbose, Sigrin & O’Shaughnessy (2023)
Journal / Source: Scientific Reports, 13:7213 (2023), Springer Nature (Nature Portfolio), DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-33014-4
Objective: To demonstrate the value of shifting from significance-based methods (logistic regression) to prediction-oriented machine learning (XGBoost) for identifying likely residential PV adopters and non-adopters, in order to reduce PV soft costs (specifically customer acquisition costs) and uncover new market opportunities for PV installation companies.
Methodology: Logistic regression used as the significance-based baseline; XGBoost (eXtreme Gradient Boosting) used as the primary prediction-oriented ML model, with Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation (R package ParBayesianOptimization) tuning tree depth, eta, gamma, min child weight, column/row sampling ratios and boosting rounds. 80/20 train/test split with 5-fold cross-validation. XGBoost also benchmarked against linear/quadratic discriminant analysis, support vector machine and random forest. A 10-scenario decomposition analysis (restraining colsample, rounds, and tree depth) was designed to isolate how much of XGBoost’s performance edge comes from variable interaction versus nonlinearity. xgboostExplainer used to interpret marginal feature impacts at the leaf level.
Key Findings: Highly significant explanatory variables are not necessarily good predictors — e.g., summer bill and income differ significantly between adopters/non-adopters (p<0.01) but individually predict adoption only marginally better than chance (~58–62%). Machine learning’s advantage stems from capturing complex variable interactions (e.g., non-linear joint effects of income and electricity bill) and nonlinear effects (U-shaped/curvilinear relationships for bill, income, and age) that logistic regression’s linear-log-odds assumption cannot represent. XGBoost implicitly recovers latent geographic (state/county) information without needing explicit location dummy variables. Using XGBoost predictions to prioritise sales visits can reduce customer acquisition costs by about $390 per installation (~15%, or $0.07/Watt). XGBoost also uncovers previously overlooked market segments (grouped by income, bill level, capacity factor/irradiation, and age) that logistic regression misses. Predictive accuracy was found to be maintained (even improved) across income deciles, suggesting ML-based targeting could help "seed" adoption in disadvantaged communities rather than worsening inequality, provided predicted non-adopters are not simply abandoned (an "information cocoon" risk the authors explicitly address).
Limitations / Gaps: Data are not a random national sample and are confined to four states, limiting generalisability, though robustness checks suggest resilience; only cross-sectional data (2014–2015) available, so the model’s predictive stability over time could not be fully tested (though predictive power was observed to increase from 2011 to 2015 within the sample); deliberately excludes subjective/attitudinal variables (e.g., environmental attitudes, willingness to pay green premiums) that could improve accuracy further but raise data-collection costs; small-sample overfitting risk is a general concern the authors flag for the broader adoption literature.
Future Work: Incorporate subjective/attitudinal variables (e.g., green premiums consumers are willing to pay, responsible electricity-consumption behaviours) to further improve predictive performance; test behavioural nudging tools (monetary and non-monetary) to convert predicted adopters; extend machine-learning adoption-prediction approaches to other distributed energy technologies (batteries, EVs, heat pumps); apply predictive "seeding" strategies to target disadvantaged/low-income communities and improve equity in subsidy design; use predictive models to support grid-infrastructure planning and transmission/storage siting.

title: Employing Machine Learning for Advanced Gap Imputation in Solar Power Generation Databases
text:
Title: Employing Machine Learning for Advanced Gap Imputation in Solar Power Generation Databases
Authors: Costa, Falcão, Mohamed, Annuk & Marinho (2024)
Journal / Source: Scientific Reports, 14:23801 (2024), Springer Nature (Nature Portfolio), DOI: 10.1038/s41598-024-74342-3
Objective: To evaluate and compare Random Forest and Gradient Boosting algorithms for imputing missing gaps in solar PV energy-generation time-series data, and to assess the downstream practical impact of imputation-model choice on the sizing of a coupled green-hydrogen production system (electrolyzer).
Methodology: Random Forest Regressor and Gradient Boosting Regressor (scikit-learn) trained on complete records to model the relationship between climate predictors and energy generation, then used to estimate the missing generation values. Missing predictor values imputed separately via SimpleImputer (mean). Data split into training/testing sets via train_test_split. feature_importances_ attribute used to quantify predictor importance (impurity/variance decrease for Random Forest; error-reduction contribution for Gradient Boosting). Imputed outputs then fed into a green-hydrogen sizing model (total energy generated, annual operating hours, annual energy available for electrolysis, mass of hydrogen produced, required electrolyzer power) to test downstream practical impact.
Key Findings: Solar irradiance standard deviation (a measure of intra-day variability) was overwhelmingly the most important predictor in both models (~83% relative importance in Random Forest, ~83% in Gradient Boosting), far ahead of average irradiance (~11% RF, ~16% GB); temperature, humidity and wind speed contributed only marginally (each under ~3%). Applying the two imputation models downstream to size a green-hydrogen electrolyzer produced starkly different real-world estimates: Random Forest-imputed data implied 581,103.6 kWh total generation and 14,819.6 kg of hydrogen produced (5.61 kW electrolyzer), versus 216,970.6 kWh and 5,533.3 kg for Gradient Boosting (1.92 kW electrolyzer), versus only 14,261.9 kWh and 363.7 kg if the raw data with the missing gap were used uncorrected (2.25 kW) — demonstrating that imputation-model choice can change downstream engineering/sizing conclusions by an order of magnitude.
Limitations / Gaps: Confined to a single PV plant/single location (Irecê, Bahia) in a high-irradiance equatorial climate, limiting generalisability to other climates or geographies; relatively short data record (~11 months) with only one substantial gap event; missing values in the *predictor* variables were filled with simple mean imputation, a comparatively coarse approach that could itself introduce bias; no comparison against deep-learning or generative approaches (e.g., GANs, RNNs) despite the paper’s own literature review noting GAN-based radiation imputation as a promising alternative; because the true values during the actual missing period are unknown, imputation quality could only be validated indirectly via held-out test-set metrics rather than against real missing-period ground truth.
Future Work: Extend the imputation approach to multiple PV plants/climates to test generalisability; explore deep-learning and generative (e.g., GAN-based) imputation methods as alternatives/complements to Random Forest and Gradient Boosting; conduct more detailed hyperparameter tuning and feature engineering (especially for Gradient Boosting, whose relatively weaker performance the authors attribute to insufficient tuning); extend downstream application testing beyond green-hydrogen sizing to other renewable-energy planning and operational-decision contexts.

title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Algorithms for Solar Irradiance Forecasting in Smart Grids
text:
Title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Algorithms for Solar Irradiance Forecasting in Smart Grids
Authors: Soleymani & Mohammadzadeh (2023)
Journal / Source: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2310.13791 [cs] (Oct. 2023) — not yet published in a peer-reviewed venue
Objective: To compare next-generation machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, MLP-ANN) for solar irradiance forecasting in smart grids, using Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) feature selection, Bayesian-optimized hyperparameter tuning, and testing spatial generalization across geographic locations.
Methodology: Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost (intrinsic feature importance, no separate feature selection) and MLP-ANN (requires separate feature selection). PCC used for MLP-ANN feature selection; Bayesian optimization (Gaussian Process-based) for hyperparameter tuning of all models; SHAP used for feature-importance interpretation of the Random Forest model; robustness tested via 5-fold cross-validation learning curves and multi-location testing.
Key Findings: PCC-based feature selection meaningfully improves MLP-ANN forecasting performance. SHAP analysis shows ambient temperature has the highest contribution to irradiance forecasts, followed by wind direction and humidity; time and length of day have minimal impact. Random Forest generalizes well to new locations — RMSE/MAE rise only slightly at 100 miles and more noticeably at 500 miles from the training location, but Random Forest still outperforms LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost and MLP-ANN at both distances.
Limitations / Gaps: Relies on a single data source (NSRDB, U.S.-based), limiting generalizability to other climates/regions; does not incorporate additional meteorological variables such as cloud cover, pollution index, or land-surface temperature; not yet peer-reviewed (arXiv preprint only).
Future Work: Explore alternative feature-selection methods (wrapper and filter approaches); test alternative hyperparameter-optimization techniques; incorporate additional parameters such as earth's-crust temperature, pollution index, and cloud index to further improve forecasting accuracy.

title: A Generative AI Technique for Synthesizing a Digital Twin for U.S. Residential Solar Adoption and Generation
text:
Title: A Generative AI Technique for Synthesizing a Digital Twin for U.S. Residential Solar Adoption and Generation
Authors: Kishore, Thorve & Marathe (2024)
Journal / Source: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2410.08098 [cs.AI] (Oct. 2024) — not yet published in a peer-reviewed venue
Objective: To develop a generative-AI methodology producing a highly granular (household-level, hourly) synthetic digital twin of U.S. rooftop solar adoption and PV generation, combining ML-based adopter identification, XAI-based feature analysis, and an analytical hourly generation model, then apply it in a Virginia policy case study on solar incentive equity.
Methodology: Ensemble of Random Forest, SVM, and Gradient Boosting classifiers (soft/hard voting) for household square-footage classification; XGBoost classifier with a custom weighted log-loss function and calibrated decision threshold, tuned via Bayesian optimization (Gaussian Process Regression + Expected Improvement) for solar-adopter identification; bottom-up analytical model for hourly PV energy generation based on roof geometry, tilt/azimuth, and irradiance; SHAP for explainability of state-level adoption models; CSonNet agent-based contagion-simulation framework for the policy case study.
Key Findings: Western and Northeastern U.S. states show the highest solar adoption rates, consistent with known national trends. Feature importance for adoption varies substantially by state (e.g., VA driven most by year built, NC by income and home size; TX by square footage, NY by income and bedrooms). In the Virginia policy case study, the 30% federal tax credit (Case 4) produced the largest adoption gains overall and the strongest urban LMI penetration, but total LMI rooftop adoption stayed under 1% in all scenarios because the workplace-based peer network sparsely connects LMI households, limiting social-diffusion effects.
Limitations / Gaps: Does not model extreme or atypical installation cases; assumes single tilt/azimuth per household and ignores mid-year installation timing; excludes reflected and diffuse irradiance components; the workplace-only peer network likely understates real-world diffusion within low-connectivity LMI communities; adoption-classification performance is notably weaker for Massachusetts than other states.
Future Work: Apply the framework to other states and alternative peer-network structures; incorporate richer physical effects (reflected/diffuse radiation, multiple panel orientations, shading); model coupling with other distributed energy resources (battery storage, EVs, heat pumps); test additional policy scenarios beyond tax credits for equity-focused solar deployment.

title: Solar and Wind Power Forecasting: A Comparative Review of LSTM, Random Forest, and XGBoost Models
text:
Title: Solar and Wind Power Forecasting: A Comparative Review of LSTM, Random Forest, and XGBoost Models
Authors: Mollasalehi & Farhadi (2025)
Journal / Source: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2509.24059 [eess.SY] (Sep. 2025) — not yet published in a peer-reviewed venue
Objective: To review and comparatively analyze three widely used ML/DL algorithms — LSTM, Random Forest, and XGBoost — for solar and wind power forecasting, evaluating them across research prevalence, model complexity, and computational execution time.
Methodology: Narrative literature review plus a comparative bar-chart analysis of LSTM, Random Forest, and XGBoost on three criteria drawn from the surveyed literature: research frequency (number of studies), model complexity (rated 1–10), and execution time (rated 1–10).
Key Findings: Random Forest and XGBoost offer an effective balance between predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, contributing to their widespread adoption in renewable-energy forecasting. LSTM and other deep-learning models tend to provide superior forecasting performance in the literature but at the cost of increased computational time and processing complexity. All three models are noted as effective at capturing nonlinear, weather-driven variability in solar and wind generation.
Limitations / Gaps: Purely a review with no original experiments or empirical benchmarking on real data; the complexity and execution-time 'scores' are qualitative/reviewer-assigned rather than measured; does not deeply cover other approaches such as hybrid models or transformer-based architectures; not yet peer-reviewed (arXiv preprint only).
Future Work: Apply RF, XGBoost, and LSTM to common, suitable datasets for direct empirical comparison; further evaluate their effectiveness and reliability across varying renewable-energy forecasting contexts and geographies.

title: Short-term solar energy forecasting: Integrated computational intelligence of LSTMs and GRU
text:
Title: Short-term solar energy forecasting: Integrated computational intelligence of LSTMs and GRU
Authors: Aneela Zameer, Fatima Jaffar, Farah Shahid, Muhammad Muneeb, Rizwan Khan, Rubina Nasir (2023 (Oct 4))
Journal / Source: PLOS ONE, 18(10): e0285410
Objective: To compare baseline ML regressors (Lasso/Ridge/ElasticNet/SVR) against LSTM/Bi-LSTM/GRU (and their variants and hybrids) for very-short-term (5-min) multivariate solar-energy forecasting, and to test multistep-ahead hybrids.
Methodology: Statistical/ML baseline: LASSO, Ridge, ElasticNet, SVR. Deep learning: LSTM×6 variants, Bi-LSTM×6 variants, GRU×6 variants. Hybrid: LSTM_GRU, LSTM_Bi-LSTM, Bi-LSTM_LSTM, Bi-LSTM_GRU, GRU_LSTM, GRU_Bi-LSTM. BEST: Bi-LSTM (and GRU-II near-equal) for single-step; LSTM_GRU/LSTM_Bi-LSTM often best at longer multistep horizons.. Flow: Data collection → cleaning → correlation-based feature selection → baseline ML regressors (Lasso/Ridge/ElasticNet/SVR) IN PARALLEL WITH → DL variants (LSTM/Bi-LSTM/GRU ×6 variants each) → hybrid combinations (6 pairings) → multistep (1/3/6/12/24) forecasting → RMSFE prediction intervals.
Key Findings: NONE — only a correlation heatmap for feature relevance, no SHAP/permutation importance/PDP.
Limitations / Gaps: Not stated as a distinct section; the paper already implements its own natural next steps (variant sweep + hybrid combos + multistep + prediction intervals) within the study itself.
Future Work / Adaptability: Low-Medium — architecture/evaluation only

title: Photovoltaic solar energy prediction using the seasonal-trend decomposition layer and ASOA optimized LSTM neural network model
text:
Title: Photovoltaic solar energy prediction using the seasonal-trend decomposition layer and ASOA optimized LSTM neural network model
Authors: Venkatachalam Mohanasundaram, Balamurugan Rangaswamy (2025 (Feb 3))
Journal / Source: Scientific Reports, 15:4032
Objective: To integrate Robust Seasonal-Trend Decomposition (RSTL) with an Adaptive Seagull Optimisation Algorithm (ASOA)-tuned LSTM so that SE output prediction is more accurate under noisy, non-stationary irradiance data.
Methodology: 8-way ablation: STL, LSTM(plain), STL+LSTM, RSTL+LSTM, STL+(SOA+LSTM), STL+(ASOA+LSTM), RSTL+(SOA+LSTM), RSTL+(ASOA+LSTM) [PROPOSED]. Isolates decomposition method (STL vs RSTL) × optimizer (SOA vs ASOA) independently. BEST: RSTL+(ASOA+LSTM) across every metric and split.. Flow: Data preprocessing → ELNET-BDE feature selection → RSTL decomposition (trend/seasonal/residual) → 3 separate ASOA-optimized LSTM models (one per component) → summation ŷt = ŝt+τ̂t+r̂t → evaluation vs 7 alternative model configurations.
Key Findings: NONE explicitly — ELNET-BDE selects features via "Bayesian posterior density" but no interpretable importance ranking or SHAP-style output is shown.
Limitations / Gaps: Explicit in Conclusion: refine the optimization algorithm further, combine with other state-of-the-art ML techniques, and apply the framework to other Renewable Energy Sources beyond solar.
Future Work / Adaptability: HIGH — decomposition + adaptive optimization framework + Indian data pipeline all transfer

title: Real-time solar PV generation in a building using LSTM-based time series forecasting
text:
Title: Real-time solar PV generation in a building using LSTM-based time series forecasting
Authors: C. Nithya, J. Preetha Roselyn, D. Devaraj (2024 (Sept 12))
Journal / Source: Discover Electronics, 1:19
Objective: To build a sequence-to-sequence LSTM regression model that forecasts real-time PV generation from an actual 100kW plant, after cleaning raw operational data, in order to support performance monitoring and failure detection.
Methodology: Only LSTM (sequence-to-sequence regression) is implemented; compared post-hoc in a results table to RNN and GRNN figures QUOTED FROM external literature ([ref16]), not re-run on the same data — a notably weaker baseline design than papers 1 & 2. BEST (self-reported): LSTM RNN.. Flow: Load sequence data → standardize (zero mean/unit variance) → shift sequences by 1 step (predictors/response) → define LSTM architecture (200 hidden units) → train (250 iterations) → forecast step-by-step, updating network state with OBSERVED values (not just predicted) at each step to limit compounding error.
Key Findings: NONE.
Limitations / Gaps: Brief, general statement only: PV forecasting can help maintain grid stability by predicting solar power fluctuations — no detailed future-work agenda given.
Future Work / Adaptability: Low — useful only as a simple baseline reference

title: MATNet: Multi-Level Fusion Transformer-Based Model for Day-Ahead PV Generation Forecasting
text:
Title: MATNet: Multi-Level Fusion Transformer-Based Model for Day-Ahead PV Generation Forecasting
Authors: Matteo Tortora, Francesco Conte, Gianluca Natrella, Paolo Soda (2023/2024 (arXiv v2 revised 2 Mar 2024); IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid (in press / early access))
Journal / Source: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid
Objective: To propose MATNet, a novel self-attention transformer architecture that combines the DL paradigm with the prior physical knowledge of PV generation (via fused historical+forecast weather branches) for more accurate, robust multivariate multi-step day-ahead PV forecasting, evaluated on the Ausgrid benchmark.
Methodology: Proposed: MATNet (self-attention transformer with multi-level fusion). Internal ablation baselines (identical fusion/output architecture, attention swapped for a recurrent layer): LSTM-, GRU-, BiLSTM-, BiGRU-based MATNet. External SOTA comparators (different train/test protocols, same Ausgrid dataset): LsSVR ensemble, Bayesian BiLSTM, Improved-Bayesian BiLSTM. BEST: attention-based MATNet outperforms every recurrent variant and every external SOTA method across RMSE/MAE/WMAPE/MASE (statistically significant, Diebold-Mariano p<0.01).. Flow: Raw PV + historical weather + forecast weather → 1D-conv Embedding Module (per-branch, kernel=3 for PV / kernel=1 for weather, projects to d_model) → sinusoidal Positional Encoding (added) → stacked (L=3) Self-Attention Transformer Encoder per branch → learnable Dense Interpolation Layer (per branch, summarizes sequence into a single d_model vector) → Multi-Level Joint Fusion (concatenate PV-history + weather-history first "early" level → dense+ReLU+dropout → concatenate with weather-forecast representation at a "later" level → dense+ReLU+dropout) → final dropout+Linear+Sigmoid output layer → 24-hour PV forecast.
Key Findings: Partial — attention weights and the learnable Dense Interpolation Layer's edge weights are visualized (Fig. 3) to show which time steps matter, but this is illustrative rather than a systematic feature-importance analysis; no SHAP/permutation importance.
Limitations / Gaps: Explicit: develop an adaptive joint-fusion layer that dynamically re-weights the three input branches (giving more weight to the weather-forecast branch specifically under adverse conditions); incorporate an eXplainable-AI paradigm into the framework to support power-system stakeholder decision-making.
Future Work / Adaptability: Medium-High — fusion architecture and branch-ablation design are highly transferable, but the paper is generation-specific with no policy features

title: A hybrid forecasting model using LSTM and Prophet for energy consumption with decomposition of time series data
text:
Title: A hybrid forecasting model using LSTM and Prophet for energy consumption with decomposition of time series data
Authors: Serdar Arslan (2022 (Jun 10))
Journal / Source: PeerJ Computer Science, 8:e1001
Objective: To develop an efficient hybrid forecasting framework hybridizing a recurrent neural network (stacked BiLSTM) with Facebook's Prophet, using STL decomposition to reduce the impact of irregular fluctuations on the neural branch while Prophet preserves seasonality, and to test it on real-world monthly consumption data for seven countries against several state-of-the-art methods.
Methodology: Statistical/other: Prophet (trend+seasonality+holidays), ARIMA, SVR, Holt-Winters (external SOTA comparators). Deep learning: stacked Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), deseasonalized BiLSTM (deBiLSTM). Hybrid (proposed): Prophet + STL-decomposed BiLSTM, combined by equal-weight averaging. External SOTA (deep/signal-processing): EMD-LSTM, EMD-GRU. BEST: no single winner — proposed Hybrid best for 5/7 countries (Canada, France, Japan, Mexico, Italy); Prophet alone best for Turkey; BiLSTM/deBiLSTM alone best for Brazil.. Flow: Original monthly data → [Path A] fit Prophet directly on the original series (captures trend gt + seasonality st + holidays ht) ; [Path B] STL Decomposition → Trend + Seasonal + Residual components → Trend & Residual fed to stacked Bidirectional LSTM → Reseasonalization (add the extracted Seasonal component back to the LSTM output) → Final forecast = equal-weight combination of Prophet's output and the reseasonalized-BiLSTM output.
Key Findings: NONE — expected, since the model is entirely univariate (only the target series itself is used as input, so there are no external features to rank).
Limitations / Gaps: Explicit: use different data sources with different seasonality patterns; adapt various additional types of RNNs (beyond stacked BiLSTM) to further explore the generalization and optimization of the hybrid mechanism.
Future Work / Adaptability: Medium — the decomposition + hybrid-ensembling concept transfers well conceptually, but the model is purely univariate

title: Solar Irradiance Forecasting Using Temporal Fusion Transformers
text:
Title: Solar Irradiance Forecasting Using Temporal Fusion Transformers
Authors: Abdulaziz Alorf, Muhammad Usman Ghani Khan (2025 (published; received Dec 2023, revised Sep 2024, accepted Oct 2024))
Journal / Source: International Journal of Energy Research, Volume 2025, Article ID 3534500
Objective: To enhance the accuracy and dependability of solar irradiance predictions, including under missing-data conditions, by combining VMD (for noise-robust decomposition of GHI into intrinsic mode functions) with a modified TFT that replaces the LSTM encoder-decoder with GRU, and to benchmark it against ANN, LSTM, CNN-LSTM, CNN-LSTM-t, a vanilla Transformer, and the original TFT.
Methodology: Baselines (all run on the identical dataset/protocol): ANN, LSTM, GRU, CNN–LSTM, CNN–LSTM with temporal attention (CNN–LSTM-t), vanilla Transformer, original TFT (LSTM-based, Lim et al. 2021). Proposed: modified/"Proposed" TFT (VMD + GRU-based encoder-decoder + variable screening network + multi-horizon fusion multihead attention). BEST: Proposed TFT wins on MAE, MSE, and R² across all four forecasting-window sizes, beating every baseline including the original TFT.. Flow: Raw dataset → Data preprocessing (datetime conversion, drop unnamed columns, missing-value averaging, nighttime-hour removal) → Feature selection (DHI, DNI, WS, WD, WD_std, T_amb, GHI) → VMD decomposition of GHI into IMFs → Forecasting-window construction (past-sequence + future-horizon pairs) → Modified TFT: Variable Screening Network → GRU-based Encoder–Decoder (replacing LSTM) → Static Enrichment (GRN) → Masked Interpretable Multi-Head Self-Attention → Position-wise Feed-Forward → Temporal Fusion Decoder → Dense layer → Quantile forecasts (10th/50th/90th percentile) → Evaluation (MAE, MSE, R²).
Key Findings: Partial — the architecture's Variable Screening Network inherently produces per-feature, per-time-step importance weights (softmax-based h_t), and quantile outputs (10th/50th/90th) give uncertainty-aware interpretability; however, the paper does not report or analyze the actual learned attention/variable weights as results (a capability left unexploited).
Limitations / Gaps: Explicit: increase the scope of the data used (more stations/regions) or experiment with different time scales/longer time intervals. Implicit (from Conclusion): analyze attention-weight patterns to study consistent seasonal temporal patterns in irradiance data, potentially increasing forecasting confidence among domain experts.
Future Work / Adaptability: HIGH — the modified TFT (GRU + variable screening network + quantile output) is one of the strongest adoption-forecasting backbone candidates seen so far; VMD decomposition and built-in interpretability are both directly reusable

title: An empirical study of consumer adoption and satisfaction of grid-connected rooftop solar among households in Rohtak division
text:
Title: An empirical study of consumer adoption and satisfaction of grid-connected rooftop solar among households in Rohtak division
Authors: Sunny Hooda; Dr. Rajesh Kumar (2025)
Journal / Source: International Journal of Political Science and Governance, 7(12), 149-155
Objective: To measure consumer satisfaction, difficulty faced during installation, reasons for installation, and awareness of rooftop solar among Rohtak Division households. (Problem: Despite policy support, household experience of grid-connected rooftop solar (cost, satisfaction, difficulties, awareness) at the regional level is under-documented, particularly in Haryana's Rohtak Division.)
Methodology: Descriptive/analytical design; percentage & mean statistical tools on survey responses. Data: Primary — structured questionnaire, random + systematic sampling
Key Findings: Households in Rohtak overwhelmingly chose medium-capacity systems (3-6kW = 84% combined), spent ₹1-3 lakh (88% cumulative), and received subsidies at very high rates (92.3%). Payback was achieved within 5 years for 80.9% of respondents. The dominant adoption driver was reducing electricity bills (66.6%), well ahead of self-dependency (16.6%) or environmental motives (~17% combined). Installation was largely trouble-free (66.6% reported no difficulty), and overall satisfaction was high (68.6% satisfied/fully satisfied vs 16.9% dissatisfied). The authors conclude adoption is primarily an economic/financial decision, not a symbolic or environmental one.
Limitations / Gaps: Not explicitly stated as a limitations section; implied by scope: single-region (Rohtak Division), descriptive statistics only (percentage/mean), no inferential modelling.. Research Gap: No state-level comparison; no predictive model; no PM Surya Ghar-specific structural analysis (scheme mentioned only in passing/keywords).
Future Work: Adaptability to PM Surya Ghar national/state monitoring

title: Economic Viability and Policy-Driven Adoption of Rooftop Solar Systems in India: A State-Level Comparative Analysis
text:
Title: Economic Viability and Policy-Driven Adoption of Rooftop Solar Systems in India: A State-Level Comparative Analysis
Authors: Avirup Mukherjee; Sidharth Raja Halder (2025)
Journal / Source: Shodh Manjusha: An International Multidisciplinary Journal, 02(02), 212-227
Objective: (1) Evaluate economic viability of rooftop solar via income, tariffs, urbanization; (2) Examine impact of financial/policy incentives (subsidies) on adoption; (3) Identify inter-state variation and policy implications. (Problem: Rooftop solar adoption varies significantly across Indian states and is not clearly explained by income or subsidy levels alone, pointing to structural/implementation gaps in policy design.)
Methodology: Descriptive statistics → Pearson correlation → Multiple Linear Regression (OLS) → ANOVA (high vs low subsidy groups). Data: Secondary — MNRE reports, SERC tariff data, state budget/policy docs, Census 2011 & MoSPI
Key Findings: Across 10 states, installations vary widely (104,886 to 263,458) and this variation is not well explained by the economic/policy variables tested. Subsidy percentage shows a moderate NEGATIVE correlation with installations (-0.62) and a near-significant negative regression coefficient — the opposite of the expected direction. Tariff, urbanization, and income show only weak positive correlations (0.28, 0.23, 0.18) and none are statistically significant predictors (all p>0.05). ANOVA confirms no significant difference in mean installations between high- and low-subsidy state groups (p=0.207). The authors conclude that policy execution quality, administrative transparency, and consumer awareness matter more than the nominal size of financial incentives — subsidies alone are 'insufficient to drive adoption.'
Limitations / Gaps: Authors explicitly note small sample size (n=10 states) limits statistical power; note multicollinearity is not high but caution is still advised.. Research Gap: No time-series/panel data (authors explicitly recommend this for future research); no household-level or socioeconomic granularity; does not incorporate PM Surya Ghar-specific implementation variables (conversion ratio, disbursement speed).
Future Work: Adaptability to PM Surya Ghar national/state monitoring

title: Gujarat's Solar Revolution: A Comprehensive Analysis of the Implementation of Solar Roof Top System Under PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijali Yojna
text:
Title: Gujarat's Solar Revolution: A Comprehensive Analysis of the Implementation of Solar Roof Top System Under PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijali Yojna
Authors: Utpal D Patel; Dr. Rajiv Patel; Dr. Satish Patel (2025)
Journal / Source: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR), 14(12), 1768-1774
Objective: To assess the actual status of RTS adoption in Gujarat, analyse roll-out and outcomes, and scrutinize persistent post-implementation challenges (subsidies, grid management, consumer behaviour), using a comparative state lens against PMSGY. (Problem: Despite Gujarat's leading rooftop solar policy legacy, persistent implementation issues (subsidy delay, financing, grid integration) remain unaddressed, and the newly launched PM Surya Ghar scheme's alignment with existing state policy is untested.)
Methodology: Desk research: keyword-based literature screening (grey + peer-reviewed) → data review/synthesis → comparative state analysis → payback-period modelling from MNRE benchmark assumptions. Data: Secondary/desk research — GEDA, MNRE, CEEW reports, PMSGY portal, SERC/state policy docs
Key Findings: Nationally, only 34.53% of PMSGY applications converted to actual installations (18.78 lakh of 54.42 lakh applications) as of the November 2025 snapshot — meaning nearly two-thirds of applicants do not complete installation. Gujarat is the standout performer (85.91% conversion, plus highest absolute application and installation volumes), while Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Andhra Pradesh, Sikkim, Karnataka, West Bengal, and Odisha show conversion ratios of just 1-13%. Large, high-volume states show mixed results: Uttar Pradesh converts under 30% despite the most applications, while Maharashtra converts nearly 60%. Financially, combined central + state subsidies dramatically cut payback period — from 32 months (no state subsidy) to as low as 0 months (Goa, with high state support). Every additional ₹10,000/kW subsidy shortens payback by roughly 5 months. Despite Gujarat's strong legacy, persistent issues remain: subsidy disbursement delays (6-8 months), rural outreach gaps, and technical bottlenecks (grid instability, inverter maintenance).
Limitations / Gaps: Authors note research gaps in the literature they reviewed (few studies on post-installation challenges, subsidy delay, maintenance) rather than limitations of their own desk-research method explicitly, though the method itself (grey + peer-reviewed literature synthesis) carries an implicit reliance on secondary reporting accuracy.. Research Gap: Few studies compare state-led vs central schemes rigorously (a gap this paper explicitly tries to address); post-installation service/maintenance quality remains under-researched; DCR mandate's real-world supply impact not yet empirically measured.
Future Work: Adaptability to PM Surya Ghar national/state monitoring

title: Residential Rooftop Solar under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (PMSG-MBY) — Export Billing Meets Time-of-Day Tariffs
text:
Title: Residential Rooftop Solar under PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (PMSG-MBY) — Export Billing Meets Time-of-Day Tariffs
Authors: Nishant Chadha (2025)
Journal / Source: Independent working paper (author's personal capacity)
Objective: To document current export-settlement mechanisms across 30+ state policies, highlight state-specific ToD/net-billing innovations, and analyse economic implications for prosumers as retail tariffs and export credits diverge. (Problem: As net-metering nationally shifts toward net billing and mandatory Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs roll out, the economics of exported rooftop solar generation for PMSG-MBY prosumers is a critical but under-explored policy intersection.)
Methodology: Policy/regulatory document review and synthesis; comparative tabulation of settlement cycles, compensation bases, and ToD designs across states. Data: Secondary — 30+ state policies, SERC tariff orders, draft regulations, PIB releases, RDSS/Prayas smart-meter data, Mercom/CEEW industry trackers
Key Findings: India's grid-connected solar base reached ~110.9 GW by June 2025; PMSG-MBY had generated >47.3 lakh applications, ₹4,770 crore disbursed to 6.13 lakh beneficiaries, and over 10 lakh homes solarised by March 2025. Settlement mechanisms are highly fragmented: 21 states use annual settlement vs 6 monthly vs 1 half-yearly; compensation bases split across APPC-linked (6 states), SERC-tariff-linked (7), bid-tariff-linked (5), and hybrid (3) methods; 12 states/UTs have already moved to net billing. As mandatory Time-of-Day tariffs roll out nationally (all non-agricultural consumers by April 2025, contingent on smart metering), mid-day solar exports will be credited at a LOWER rate than before, shrinking per-unit export value and shifting the economic logic toward self-consumption/load-shifting and storage rather than pure export. This shift is jeopardized by very low smart-meter communication rates (~10% of sanctioned meters actively reporting as of July 2025) and a DCR-driven module price premium (₹25/W vs ₹15/W imported).
Limitations / Gaps: Author explicitly frames this as a working paper with views 'solely those of the author,' implying acknowledged provisionality; does not include a formal limitations section but flags 'operational bottlenecks' as open, unresolved issues rather than settled findings.. Research Gap: Does not quantify the household-level financial impact of ToD-linked export devaluation (i.e., no household payback-period recalculation under new ToD rules) — a natural extension for a forecasting project. Limited discussion of consumer behavioural response to ToD signals.
Future Work: Adaptability to PM Surya Ghar national/state monitoring

title: Power on the Roof: Reviewing Rooftop Solar Adoption in India
text:
Title: Power on the Roof: Reviewing Rooftop Solar Adoption in India
Authors: Saithu Mohammed; P. Maheswari (2025)
Journal / Source: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Applied Science (IJRIAS), X(IX), 413-422
Objective: To synthesize peer-reviewed and grey literature (2019-2025) on trends, barriers, enablers, economics, regional signals, stakeholder outcomes, and policy implications for RTS adoption in India, and set a future research agenda. (Problem: Despite ambitious national targets and technical potential, rooftop solar adoption in India has consistently lagged, and the drivers (barriers, enablers, business models, regional variation) are fragmented across the literature.)
Methodology: Narrative (non-systematic, non-meta-analytic) literature synthesis structured by theme: policy landscape → adoption trends → barriers → enablers → business models → regional cases → stakeholders → research gaps. Data: Secondary — narrative review of peer-reviewed literature (2019-2025), government program documents, policy reports (CEEW, IEEFA, ADBI, MNRE, PIB)
Key Findings: Synthesizing 2019-2025 literature, the review finds India's cumulative rooftop capacity (~16.3 GW by early 2025) remains well below both the original 40 GW/2022 National Solar Mission target and the >200 GW technical potential. Adoption has historically concentrated in the commercial/industrial segment (favorable tariffs, credit access), with residential uptake accelerating only after PM Surya Ghar's 2024 launch. Five states — Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu — account for ~70% of all rooftop capacity; Gujarat alone held >60% of India's cumulative RESIDENTIAL rooftop capacity by FY2022. Persistent barriers cluster into five types: finance/affordability, regulatory uncertainty, procedural friction, information/trust deficits, and built-environment constraints. Emerging enablers — slab-based subsidies, digital portals, DISCOM performance incentives, vendor certification, and collateral-free credit — are beginning to shift the dynamic. Regional case studies (Gujarat=policy depth, Maharashtra=regulatory volatility risk, Kerala=utility-led SOURA promise/limits, Uttar Pradesh=ecosystem-development challenge) show adoption depends as much on subnational institutional capacity as on national policy design.
Limitations / Gaps: Authors explicitly state: literature is dynamic (frequent net-metering/subsidy revisions may not be captured); coverage is uneven across states (disproportionate focus on Gujarat/Maharashtra); this is a narrative, not systematic/meta-analytic, review — emphasizing breadth/synthesis over statistical aggregation.. Research Gap: Explicitly names five future-research priorities: (1) causal/quasi-experimental evaluation of specific program features (DISCOM incentives, digital portals); (2) systematic evaluation of financing innovations (interest subvention, credit guarantees); (3) grid integration (hosting capacity, smart metering, ToD, storage); (4) apartment/collective housing governance models; (5) quality assurance/installer performance evidence base.
Future Work: Adaptability to PM Surya Ghar national/state monitoring

title: Antecedents Affecting Consumer's Intention to use Solar Panel in India: A Way for Green Energy
text:
Title: Antecedents Affecting Consumer's Intention to use Solar Panel in India: A Way for Green Energy
Authors: Monika Mittal, Kasturi Upadhay (2024)
Journal / Source: European Economic Letters, Vol 14, Issue 2
Objective: Identify antecedents of consumer intention to use solar panels in India across environmental, economic, and social dimensions; assess awareness-to-usage gap and insurance protection gap.
Methodology: EFA/Principal Component Analysis: KMO=0.607-0.8, Bartlett's p<0.05, 2-factor solution (Buyer-side barriers alpha=0.588; Supplier/Insurance-side barriers alpha=0.588), explains 64.5% variance. No regression/predictive model used - descriptive/exploratory only.. Flow: Survey (Saunders Research Onion, pragmatic/deductive) -> SPSS EFA (varimax rotation) -> Demographic cross-tabulations (age/occupation/marital status/education x awareness x usage) -> Recommendations
Key Findings: Awareness -> Positive but insufficient (98.9% aware, only 27% use). Income/Education -> Insignificant (unusual vs other literature). Aesthetics/roof damage -> Strong negative (high factor loadings 0.76-0.79). Subsidy -> Positive but not quantified causally.. 182/184 (98.9%) aware of solar panels, but only 50/184 (27%) actually use them - a stark awareness-to-action gap. Only ~1% of adopters carry solar insurance - major protection gap. Two-factor barrier structure: Buyer-side (funds/knowledge/time) and Supplier-side (service/claims/distribution).
Limitations / Gaps: Barriers: High upfront/installation cost; perceived aesthetic unattractiveness ('ugly', roof damage risk); lack of product knowledge; poor information dissemination; weak/complex solar-insurance claims process; poor distribution channels for insurance products.. Limitations: Study limited to non-solar-panel users in India only; other states/countries not covered; recommends expanding to other target groups in future research.. Gap: No state-level forecasting model; no predictive/quantitative adoption modeling; no policy-scenario simulation; treats adoption only as static awareness/usage snapshot, not a forecastable/time-based process.
Future Work: Explore innovative ways to overcome barriers; expand to other user segments/geographies; enhance green energy adoption strategies.

title: Understanding Consumer Adoption of Renewable Energy Technologies in Rajasthan: A Case-Based Empirical Investigation of Solar Panels
text:
Title: Understanding Consumer Adoption of Renewable Energy Technologies in Rajasthan: A Case-Based Empirical Investigation of Solar Panels
Authors: Saraswati Kumari, J.K. Tandon (2025)
Journal / Source: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Applied Science (IJRIAS), Vol X, Issue VIII
Objective: (1) Analyze socio-economic, psychological, and policy-related determinants of adoption; (2) examine the mediating role of environmental concern and moderating role of policy awareness in the relationship between perceived barriers (cost, risk) and adoption intention.
Methodology: EFA/CFA (good model fit: CFI=0.94, RMSEA=0.05); SEM (Environmental Concern beta=0.48, Risk beta=-0.30, Economic Barriers beta=-0.42, all significant); Hierarchical Regression (Base R2=0.53 with Income/Education/Policy Awareness; Extended R2=0.59 adding Environmental Concern, +0.06 incremental); Conjoint Analysis (Long-Term Savings utility=4.5, Efficiency=4.2 vs Initial Cost=2.1, Maintenance=2.3); Cluster Analysis (3 profiles: cost-sensitive/uninformed, moderately aware, highly aware/environmentally motivated - the latter unexpectedly shows LOWEST adoption intention 1.91, likely risk-offset).. Flow: Household survey (stratified sample) -> EFA (3 constructs: Environmental Awareness, Economic Barriers, Risk & Policy Awareness) -> CFA (CFI=0.94, RMSEA=0.05) -> SEM (path coefficients) -> Conjoint Analysis (attribute utilities) -> Hierarchical Regression -> Mediation/Moderation tests -> Cluster Analysis (3 segments)
Key Findings: Environmental Concern -> Positive, beta=0.48, p<0.01 (strongest driver). Economic Barriers -> Negative, beta=-0.42, p<0.01. Perceived Risk -> Negative, beta=-0.30, p<0.05. Policy Awareness -> Positive moderator (weakens risk's negative effect). Income/Education -> Positive, significant.. Environmental concern (0.48) > Economic barriers (-0.42) > Perceived risk (-0.30) in relative influence magnitude. R2 improves from 0.53 to 0.59 (+6%) adding environmental concern - meaningful predictive gain. Only 32.5% full policy awareness despite strong state subsidy programs - real communication gap. 3 distinct consumer segments identified for targeted outreach.
Limitations / Gaps: Barriers: Upfront capital cost, long payback periods, limited financing access, vendor/technology trust deficits, weak post-installation service network, fragmented information ecosystem, psychological inertia and skepticism about policy durability.. Limitations: Small sample (n=100); single-region (Rajasthan only); cross-sectional design (no longitudinal tracking); measures self-reported adoption INTENTION rather than actual installed adoption behavior.. Gap: No state-level adoption FORECASTING model (only intention, not realized/time-series adoption); not scenario-based (no explicit 'what-if policy X changes' simulation capability); single-state, small-sample - not built for cross-state or national-level generalization.
Future Work: Incorporate longitudinal data to track behaviour over time; include peer influence, media exposure, installation-experience variables; extend to rural settings and commercial users.

title: Rooftop and Community Solar Adoption with Income Heterogeneity
text:
Title: Rooftop and Community Solar Adoption with Income Heterogeneity
Authors: Swapnil Rayal, Apurva Jain, Matthew Lorig (2024)
Journal / Source: arXiv preprint (econ.GN), University of Washington (Foster School of Business / Applied Mathematics)
Objective: Develop a bilevel optimization model where households solve an optimal-stopping problem (if/when/which product to adopt, given income-dependent discount rate and demand growth) and a central planner sets subsidy levels to minimize total subsidy cost subject to adoption-level and time constraints.
Methodology: Stochastic calculus (Ito diffusion, optimal stopping, Dynkin's formula); convex optimization (proven convex for homogeneous subsidy; non-convex for heterogeneous, solved via grid search); closed-form derivation of adoption-time probability density (Lemma 4, extended to population level via log-logistic income distribution in Lemma 8). Not statistical inference on real data - purely analytical/theoretical with numerical illustration.. Flow: Household-level: stochastic optimal-stopping problem (geometric Brownian motion demand process) -> closed-form adoption-time threshold & density function. Planner-level: bilevel/Stackelberg optimization (planner sets subsidy anticipating household response) -> convexity proof (homogeneous subsidy case) / grid-search algorithm (heterogeneous case) -> numerical simulation for policy insight.
Key Findings: Higher income -> lower discount rate -> prefers ROOFTOP solar (proven via closed-form income threshold r*(delta)). Lower income -> higher discount rate -> prefers COMMUNITY/subscription solar. Higher subsidy on either product -> shifts threshold AND accelerates adoption timing (proven monotonic). Longer time-target -> lower required subsidy cost; higher adoption-level target -> higher required cost (proven substitutes).. (1) Explicit income threshold r*(delta) separates rooftop- from community-solar-preferring households, provably monotonic in each product's subsidy level. (2) Adoption-level and adoption-time targets are cost substitutes for the planner. (3) Community-solar availability lets planners meet tight adoption targets at LOWER cost than a rooftop-only high-subsidy strategy - counter to current common policy practice.
Limitations / Gaps: Barriers: Modeled implicitly as the upfront cost gap (K+kc) that lower-income/high-discount-rate households cannot easily absorb, plus the lack of a low-upfront-cost product alternative (motivating the rooftop-vs-community comparison). No awareness/trust/aesthetic barriers considered (unlike Papers 1 & 2).. Limitations: No closed-form solution possible for generalized net-billing/no-credit compensation mechanisms (approximated via Asian-option analogies without full analytical solution); assumes full household information and rational optimal-stopping behavior - no behavioral frictions; capacity assumed identical across both products (simplification); calibrated only to US parameters.. Gap: No adoption forecasting in the empirical/ML sense (this is optimization, not prediction); no India-specific parameters at all; no incorporation of behavioral/awareness variables (which Papers 1 & 2 address); no historical/observed adoption data used anywhere - entirely theoretical/normative.
Future Work: Explore effect of specific population densities and alternative inequality measures on subsidy design; extend to more than two product types; further develop the general n-product formulation (Section 6.2) into fully solvable special cases.

title: Looking High and Low: Incentive Policies and Residential Solar Adoption in High- and Low-Income U.S. Communities
text:
Title: Looking High and Low: Incentive Policies and Residential Solar Adoption in High- and Low-Income U.S. Communities
Authors: Xiaojing Xu, Charles Sims, Chien-fei Chen, J. Scott Holladay, Gerald Jones Jr., Tim Roberson (2024)
Journal / Source: Energies (MDPI), Vol 17, Issue 18, Article 4538
Objective: To estimate the increase in residential rooftop solar adoption associated with three types of state-level solar incentive programs (net metering NM, property tax incentives PTI, low-income assistance LIA) and to isolate/compare the effect of each program type in high-income versus low-and-moderate-income (LMI) census tracts across the entire contiguous U.S., using two different LMI thresholds (<120% and <80% of area median income).
Methodology: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression with state-clustered standard errors; log-linear specification (natural log of adoption rate + small constant); two model specifications - Model 1 pools all LIA-adopting states into a single dummy, Model 2 uses individual state dummies for the 8 states with LIA programs (CA, CT, IL, MA, MN, NV, NY, OR) to capture state-level heterogeneity; policy variables interacted with an LMI dummy to test differential effects; estimated separately for two LMI definitions and for three state subsamples (states with only PTI, states with only NM, states with 2+ programs). R-squared ranges 0.35-0.56 across specifications; F-statistics in the thousands indicating strong overall model significance.. Flow: DeepSolar satellite image classification -> census-tract-level aggregation of adoption rate -> merge with state policy-presence data, electricity price, property tax, socio-demographic and climate variables -> define LMI census tracts (two thresholds: <120% AMI and <80% AMI) -> OLS regression of ln(adoption rate + 0.001) on policy dummies interacted with LMI dummy plus controls, with standard errors clustered at the state level -> robustness checks using state subsamples (states with 1, 2, or 3+ programs) -> compute percent-change-in-adoption and adoption-gap tables.
Key Findings: NM -> Positive on adoption overall but effect is much larger in high-income tracts (90% increase) than low-income tracts (58% increase) when LMI defined as <120% AMI, meaning NM WIDENS the adoption gap. PTI -> Positive but similarly skewed toward high-income tracts (29% vs 6% increase), also WIDENS the gap. LIA -> Positive and, unusually, LARGER in low-income tracts (36%) than high-income tracts (30%) under the <120% AMI definition, meaning LIA NARROWS the gap by about 6 percentage points - the only incentive type to do so. However, under the stricter <80% AMI definition, LIA's gap-narrowing effect disappears entirely (both groups ~37%, interaction term not significant), and PTI actually REDUCES adoption by 3.5% in the very poorest tracts, suggesting property-value/tax-capitalization effects may deter the lowest-income households specifically.. Table 1: adoption rate summary statistics by income group (% no-adoption tracts: 31.6% low-income vs 12.4% high-income; median adoption 0.0012 low vs 0.0040 high). Table 3: full OLS regression coefficients showing NM, PTI positively significant (p<0.001) with negative LMI-interaction terms (gap-widening); LIA positive with a small but significant positive LMI-interaction under the loose definition (gap-narrowing) that becomes insignificant under the strict definition. Table 4: percent-increase-in-adoption summary by policy and income group. Table 5: state-subsample regressions showing incentive effects are somewhat larger (2-9 percentage points) when estimated on more comparable state subsamples rather than the full 49-state sample, implying some selection bias in prior single-state/small-sample causal studies.
Limitations / Gaps: Barriers: High upfront/installation cost (implicit rationale for all three incentive types); credit constraints and lower homeownership rates among LMI households (cited from prior literature as adoption barriers); risk of cross-subsidization where LMI ratepayers indirectly subsidize wealthier NM adopters' bill credits; possible property-value/tax-capitalization effects that could make PTI actively unattractive for the poorest homeowners (a novel finding, not simply an absence-of-benefit); data/research gap - prior causal literature almost exclusively studied high-adoption, high-income states, leaving policy effectiveness in poorer regions (e.g., U.S. South) essentially unstudied prior to this paper.. Limitations: Cross-sectional (2015 snapshot) data prevents causal identification of policy impacts - no before/after comparison possible; dataset does not capture the SIZE or generosity of incentives, only their presence/absence; local/city-level incentive programs are excluded from the analysis (only 4 existed nationally by 2015, so this is a minor omission); electricity bill assistance programs (e.g., LIHEAP) are deliberately excluded even though they may depress solar demand among LMI households who might otherwise view solar as a bill-reduction tool; utilities were only beginning to track time-series solar adoption data as of the study period, precluding panel/longitudinal analysis.. Gap: No adoption forecasting model (purely cross-sectional/descriptive, not predictive of future adoption); no India-specific analysis or parameters at all; does not model individual household-level decision factors such as awareness, trust, or attitudes (a structural gap addressed by the qualitative papers in this batch); introduces a genuinely novel and underused analytical frame - explicitly distinguishing 'does the policy raise LMI adoption' from 'does the policy narrow the LMI adoption gap' - which is largely absent from the other reviewed papers and is highly relevant for evaluating equity claims made about PM Surya Ghar.
Future Work: Authors note that as more U.S. utilities begin collecting time-series solar adoption data (many were only starting to do so as of the study period), it will become possible to estimate the CAUSAL effect of incentive policies using before/after or panel designs - the current cross-sectional results are explicitly framed as a first step to help prioritize where such causal research should focus. They also recommend future data collection on the actual MAGNITUDE/generosity of incentives (dollar value, eligibility caps, income thresholds) rather than simple presence/absence, which would sharpen the analysis considerably.

title: Shady solar: understanding barriers and facilitators to residential solar adoption for low- and moderate-income homeowners in New York City
text:
Title: Shady solar: understanding barriers and facilitators to residential solar adoption for low- and moderate-income homeowners in New York City
Authors: Aditi Bansal, Casey Dean, Ellie Kahn, Daphany Rose Sanchez, Diana Hernandez (2024)
Journal / Source: Frontiers in Energy Research, Vol 12, Article 1293291
Objective: To draw on interviews with LMI homeowners, program implementers, and policymakers/advocates to identify barriers and facilitators to inclusive residential solar adoption in NYC, characterize misalignments in perspective across these stakeholder groups, and generate evidence-based, actionable policy recommendations for a more equitable solar transition.
Methodology: None - this is a purely qualitative study with no regression, econometric, or statistical significance testing of any kind; no sentiment-scoring algorithm is used (unlike the Kerala paper in this batch); analytic rigor is instead established through NVivo-assisted systematic coding, iterative comparison across transcripts, peer debriefing, and member-checking (sharing summarized findings back with some participants to validate interpretations).. Flow: Community-engaged co-design between ElectrifyNYC program partners and academic research team -> drafting of three stakeholder-specific semi-structured interview guides -> purposive participant recruitment and income/interest-based screening -> 26 audio-recorded virtual interviews conducted across the three stakeholder groups -> verbatim transcription -> import into NVivo -> Phase 1 'open coding' (descriptive) -> development of a shared codebook -> Phase 2 'axial coding' (thematic grouping across transcripts) -> synthesis into a cross-group barriers/facilitators summary table (Table 2) with supporting exemplary quotes (Tables 3-4) -> derivation of 6 evidence-based policy recommendations.
Key Findings: High upfront cost -> Negative (dominant, universally cited financial deterrent, especially salient given LMI households' lower disposable income). Legacy of distrust (ESCOs/utilities/solar companies) -> Negative (reduces willingness to engage with any solar offer, regardless of underlying economics). Economic and administrative burden -> Negative for BOTH homeowners (research/paperwork fatigue) and implementers (uncompensated staff time for high-touch community engagement) - a barrier that manifests differently by stakeholder type but is structurally the same root cause. Misaligned tax-credit design (non-refundable, tax-liability-dependent) -> Negative specifically for LMI households, identified independently by both implementers and policymakers as the single most consequential structural policy flaw. Credit-score/financing requirements -> Negative, and disproportionately so for Black and Latinx households given documented credit-score disparities. Growing energy burden -> Positive motivator (drives initial interest in solar as a bill-stabilization tool). Environmental stewardship/conservation ethic -> Positive motivator. Community-based, trusted implementation (CBOs) -> Positive facilitator (rebuilds trust, increases uptake likelihood). External advocacy pressure -> Positive facilitator at the policymaking level (helped pass CLCPA, sustains accountability pressure on agencies).. Table 2 (source paper) summarizes barriers and facilitators separately for each of the three stakeholder groups, revealing that 'economic and administrative burden' is the one barrier category common to BOTH homeowners AND implementers, though it manifests very differently (personal financial/paperwork burden for homeowners vs. uncompensated organizational staff-time burden for implementers) - an important finding about how the SAME root structural problem produces different downstream effects depending on stakeholder position. Homeowner barriers: high upfront cost, legacy of distrust, administrative burden. Implementer barriers: misaligned policy design, administrative burden, information gaps (including a notable finding that implementers often UNDERESTIMATE how much LMI consumers already know about solar, especially in immigrant communities with prior exposure to solar in their countries of origin). Policymaker barriers: insufficient LMI tax appetite, monopoly of private developer/utility interests in the policymaking process. Facilitators: growing energy burden and environmental stewardship (homeowners); motivated consumers and holistic, workforce-development-linked community approaches (implementers); external advocacy pressure that helped pass and now helps enforce the CLCPA (policymakers).
Limitations / Gaps: Barriers: A structured, separately catalogued list distinct from the barrier THEMES: High upfront cost (Financial; affects LMI homeowners most; High impact); Legacy of distrust in ESCOs/utilities/solar companies (Social/Psychological; affects LMI homeowners; High impact); Economic and administrative burden of navigating incentives and vetting vendors (Administrative; affects both homeowners and implementers; High impact); Misaligned/non-refundable tax-credit policy design (Policy; affects LMI specifically; High impact); Credit-score and financing access barriers (Financial; disproportionately affects Black and Latinx households; High impact); Information gaps regarding eligibility and available incentives (Informational; affects homeowners; Medium-High impact); Insufficient tax appetite among LMI households to monetize non-refundable credits (Policy; LMI specifically; High impact); Capture of the policymaking process by private developer/utility interests (Structural/Political; disadvantaged communities broadly; Medium-High impact); Top-down program design with minimal community engagement (Administrative/Design; immigrant- and CBO-served communities; Medium impact); Uncompensated CBO labor for high-touch, trust-building community engagement (Financial/Organizational; implementers specifically; Medium-High impact); Physical condition of homes/roofs (Technical; under-discussed by participants but flagged by authors as a real, likely underestimated barrier).. Limitations: Findings are geographically concentrated in and largely specific to NYC, limiting broad applicability outside this policy/regulatory context (though the authors argue NYC's advanced equity-policy environment makes it instructive for other localities designing similar programs); interviews were conducted during the city budget season, constraining the ability to recruit as many policymaker participants as intended (only 4 secured); recruitment of LMI homeowners occurred during COVID-19 social-distancing mandates, constraining interview modality and recruitment methods; the homeowner sample skews toward those already actively considering solar, so the study could not capture why some households never consider solar adoption at all; the study explicitly excluded renters, a large and policy-relevant NYC population; the study did not examine racial disparities as a primary analytic axis despite acknowledging literature linking race to solar potential and adoption gaps.. Gap: No quantitative or predictive adoption modeling of any kind (purely qualitative); does not incorporate historical or panel/time-series adoption data; does not compare across U.S. states or cities; the analytic focus is almost entirely on POLICY DESIGN, ADMINISTRATIVE PROCESS, and INSTITUTIONAL TRUST rather than techno-economic or demographic adoption drivers per se; usefully surfaces an under-examined intersection - the interaction of non-refundable tax-credit design, credit-score/racial disparities, and housing-tenure (renter) exclusion - that is largely absent from the more quantitative papers in this batch and represents a genuine equity-modeling gap worth flagging for SuryaIQ's feature engineering.
Future Work: Authors recommend conducting future interviews outside of city budget season specifically to secure fuller policymaker participation; recommend exploring the impact of the federal Inflation Reduction Act (IRA, 2022) on solar adoption and on uptake of other clean-energy technologies once its provisions (including a new direct-pay option for non-profit/public-sector actors) have had time to take effect; recommend ethnographic and observational research to triangulate self-reported interview data against actual observed behaviors and program-participation records; explicitly call for future research at the intersection of race, socioeconomic status, and homeownership status in shaping solar adoption outcomes.

title: Unveiling the shadows: a qualitative exploration of barriers to rooftop solar photovoltaic adoption in residential sectors
text:
Title: Unveiling the shadows: a qualitative exploration of barriers to rooftop solar photovoltaic adoption in residential sectors
Authors: Tony C. Mathew, Sridevi Nagaraja Pandian (2024)
Journal / Source: Clean Energy (Oxford University Press), Vol 8, No. 5, pp. 218-228
Objective: To qualitatively identify and thematically categorize the barriers to rooftop solar PV adoption among non-adopter households in Kerala via face-to-face semi-structured interviews, and to gauge overall household sentiment toward solar technology (RQ1: initial thoughts/openness) versus sentiment specifically around the barriers preventing adoption (RQ2), in order to inform targeted policy interventions and public-awareness strategies.
Methodology: No regression, econometric, or predictive statistical model of any kind is used. The only quantitative element is NVivo's built-in automated sentiment-classification tool, which assigns each coded transcript segment to one of four ordinal sentiment categories (very negative/moderately negative/moderately positive/very positive); results are reported purely as reference/mention counts per theme (Table 3: Financial 55, Information 41, Technical 37, Regulatory & Policy 19, Social 9, Psychological 8) and as sentiment-category frequency counts (Table 2 for RQ1; Fig. 2 bar chart for RQ2) - no coefficients, p-values, or model-fit statistics are computed, and no custom predictive or statistical model is built by the authors themselves.. Flow: Purposive sampling using a non-adopter inclusion criterion -> semi-structured face-to-face interviews conducted Jan-Mar 2024 across Kerala districts -> verbatim transcription -> import into NVivo 14 -> descriptive/open coding to segment data -> development of coding nodes for recurring themes -> thematic/axial coding to group related nodes -> NVivo automated sentiment analysis applied separately to RQ1 and RQ2 response segments -> data visualization via tree map (Fig. 1, RQ1 themes) and word cloud (Fig. 3, RQ2 terms) -> validity checks (cross-transcript comparison, peer review, participant validation) -> identification of 6 primary barrier themes -> policy recommendations.
Key Findings: RQ1 sentiment (general openness to solar) -> Predominantly Positive: 75% of coded responses were moderately-to-very positive about solar in principle, indicating no fundamental resistance to the technology itself. RQ2 sentiment (specifically about barriers) -> More evenly split and comparatively less positive, reflecting that real, concrete obstacles temper the generally favorable underlying attitude. Financial Barriers -> Negative and the single most dominant theme by far (55 NVivo coding references, more than any other category) - high capital cost, poor perceived ROI, and long payback period are the primary deterrents. Information Barriers -> Negative (41 references) - lack of trustworthy, accessible information specifically about microgeneration/PV systems significantly hinders informed decision-making. Technical Barriers -> Negative (37 references) - roof-space, structural, and grid-connection issues are common concerns. Regulatory & Policy Barriers -> Negative (19 references) - net-metering uncertainty and administrative complexity discourage adoption. Social Barriers -> Minor/mixed (9 references). Psychological Barriers -> Negative but smallest in volume (8 references) - tradition and switching-cost resistance play a real but comparatively minor role.. Six barrier themes identified via thematic analysis, Financial Barriers dominant at 55 references (nearly 1.5x the next-largest theme); RQ1 sentiment analysis shows 75% of responses moderately-to-very positive toward solar in general (only 7 of 28 total coded sentiment responses were negative), indicating strong latent interest; RQ2 word-cloud analysis (Fig. 3) shows 'installation,' 'cost,' 'solar panels,' 'electricity,' and 'information' as the most visually/frequency-prominent terms associated with barriers, reinforcing that financial and informational concerns dominate respondent language even more than the reference-count table alone suggests; overall narrative finding is that Kerala households are NOT fundamentally resistant to solar as a concept but are concretely blocked by a specific, rankable set of financial, informational, and technical obstacles that targeted policy could plausibly address.
Limitations / Gaps: Barriers: Six primary barrier themes, ranked by NVivo coding-reference frequency (Table 3 in source): (1) Financial Barriers (55 references) - high initial/capital cost, poor ROI, long payback, minimal cost recovery; High impact, cited as the dominant concern across nearly all respondents. (2) Information Barriers (41 references) - lack of trustworthy, accessible information specifically on microgeneration/solar PV; High impact, affects all prospective adopters regardless of interest level. (3) Technical Barriers (37 references) - inadequate roof space, structural limitations, grid-connection issues; Medium-High impact, particularly affects households with unsuitable rooftops (a meaningful subset given 90% villa-type housing in this sample).
