(4) Regulatory & Policy Barriers (19 references) - net-metering uncertainty, complex/opaque administrative procedures; Medium-High impact, discourages even otherwise-motivated households. (5) Social Barriers (9 references) - social norms, self-efficacy, peer beliefs; Low-Medium impact. (6) Psychological Barriers (8 references) - tradition, image, switching-cost resistance; Low-Medium impact, smallest of the six themes by volume but still identified as a distinct, real driver of hesitancy.. Limitations: Sample size of 52 households, while described by the authors as sufficient for qualitative analysis, may not fully capture the diversity of experiences and perspectives across Kerala's varied socioeconomic and geographic subregions, limiting generalizability even within the state; the study's geographic focus is exclusively Kerala, and findings may not directly transfer to other Indian states with different climatic, economic, or social/cultural conditions, policy environments, or energy infrastructure.. Gap: No quantitative, predictive, or forecasting modeling of any kind is attempted; no historical or panel/time-series adoption data are used or referenced; the study does not compare across Indian states, so Kerala-specific findings cannot be assumed to generalize nationally; despite naming income variation as contextually important, the paper does not incorporate any actual socioeconomic stratification into its analysis - a gap directly relevant to this batch's core research question; the paper's principal contribution is instead a rich, India-grounded, six-category barrier TAXONOMY (financial > informational > technical > regulatory > social > psychological, ranked by salience) that usefully complements the batch's more quantitative papers by supplying qualitative texture and a plausible ordinal ranking of barrier importance, even though it offers no numeric estimates that could be directly incorporated into a predictive model.
Future Work: Authors recommend comparative studies involving other Indian states or countries with higher rates of solar PV adoption to identify which barriers and facilitators are transferable versus context-specific; recommend longitudinal studies to track how adoption rates and household attitudes evolve over time, especially in response to policy changes and technological advancements; recommend deeper exploration of the psychological and sociocultural dimensions of adoption resistance, particularly the role of social norms and community influence; recommend future research that systematically evaluates the causal impact of specific government policies and incentives (rather than the purely descriptive/qualitative treatment given here) on adoption acceleration, to provide direct feedback for policy refinement.

title: The Politics of Late Late Development in Renewable Energy Sectors: Dependency and Contradictory Tensions in India’s National Solar Mission
text:
Title: The Politics of Late Late Development in Renewable Energy Sectors: Dependency and Contradictory Tensions in India’s National Solar Mission
Authors: Pritish Behuria (2020)
Journal / Source: World Development, 126, 104726 (2020), Elsevier, DOI: 10.1016/j.worlddev.2019.104726 (Open Access, CC BY)
Objective: To examine how shifts in the global political economy of the solar GPN (falling panel prices, Chinese/East Asian manufacturing dominance) have interacted with India’s domestic political economy to shape the management of deployment vs. manufacturing priorities in India’s National Solar Mission (NSM); argues India is a "late late industrializer" whose manufacturing base has been sacrificed to the goal of cheap, rapid deployment.
Methodology: Qualitative political-economy case study; semi-structured interview analysis triangulated with document/media analysis; draws on "rent management" theory (Schmitz, Johnson & Altenburg 2015; Khan 2010) and late-industrialization theory (Gerschenkron 1962) as the analytical lens. No statistical or ML modeling.
Key Findings: (1) The 2010 Domestic Content Requirement (DCR) was successfully challenged by the US at the WTO (2016 ruling against India), weakening India’s main manufacturing-support tool. (2) The 2018 "manufacturing-linked" 10 GW solar auction (targeting 3 GW of linked manufacturing) saw very limited developer interest and was repeatedly delayed. (3) The 2018 safeguard duty (25%, tapering to 15%) was undermined because SEZ-based manufacturers (including Adani’s own Mundra plant, which had lobbied for the duty) were themselves initially caught by it, causing policy confusion. (4) Reverse-auction bidding for low tariffs empowered energy developers over manufacturers, who lack comparable lobbying power. (5) India’s "late late" industrializer position (entering after China had already captured >60% of global PV manufacturing) makes catching up structurally very difficult without much stronger, sustained state support.
Limitations / Gaps: Single-country qualitative case study based on a relatively small interview sample (n=38), with possible selection bias toward accessible, English-speaking elite informants; limited by sparse academic literature on the post-2014 NSM period; offers no quantitative/statistical modeling of the tariff–manufacturing trade-off; does not examine household/consumer-level adoption dynamics at all.
Future Work: Comparative studies of other "late late developing" countries (South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa) facing similar renewable-energy manufacturing dependency; longitudinal tracking of the safeguard-duty/SEZ dispute resolution and its effects; closer examination of Balance-of-System (BOS) component manufacturing as an alternative industrial-policy target where India might realistically compete.

title: Recent Developments and Challenges in Solar Energy Utilization in India
text:
Title: Recent Developments and Challenges in Solar Energy Utilization in India
Authors: Prem Kumar & Rajesh Kumar Verma (2025)
Journal / Source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science & Engineering Technology (IJRASET), Vol. 13, Issue X, Oct 2025, pp. 618–623, DOI: 10.22214/ijraset.2025.74523
Objective: To analyze recent (through 2025) technological, economic and institutional changes in India’s solar sector; examine barriers to large-scale deployment (storage, grid, financing, imports, DISCOM health); and propose policy/technical recommendations to help India reach its 2030 solar capacity targets.
Methodology: Descriptive-analytical secondary-data synthesis; simple trend-based time-series charts (capacity growth, LCOE/module-cost decline, CO2 reduction) and a basic scenario/sensitivity projection to 2030 (baseline vs. "ambitious" policy scenarios); qualitative literature review of ML-related solar studies (e.g., perovskite/tandem cells, hybrid systems) but no original ML model built or run by the authors themselves.
Key Findings: (1) LCOE fell from Rs. 18/kWh (2010) to Rs. 2.3/kWh (2025); module costs fell similarly (Rs. 18/W → Rs. 2.5/W). (2) Deployment is geographically skewed — Rajasthan, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu dominate utility-scale capacity while eastern/northern states lag due to weaker incentives and grid issues. (3) Rooftop solar remains far below its technical potential because of financing and institutional barriers. (4) The top cited barriers are intermittency (25%), grid infrastructure (20%), import dependence (20%) and financing (20%), with land use (15%) least significant. (5) Battery storage (mainly lithium-ion), green hydrogen, DISCOM financial reform and stronger domestic manufacturing (PLI scheme) are identified as the critical levers for reaching 2030 targets.
Limitations / Gaps: Relies entirely on secondary/aggregated data (possible inconsistencies across MNRE/IEA/IRENA sources); data gaps at the sub-state level; the 2030 capacity projections ("180–240 GW", "≥280 GW") are described only as "trend-based modeling" without transparent methodological detail; published in a comparatively lower-tier, broad-scope engineering journal (IJRASET) rather than a specialized energy-policy outlet; no original primary data collection or ML/statistical modeling.
Future Work: Deeper, methodologically transparent quantitative/econometric or ML-based modeling of India’s 2030 capacity trajectory; state-level micro-studies of DISCOM financial reform impact on solar uptake; empirical evaluation of PLI-scheme effectiveness for domestic manufacturing; more granular geospatial analysis of rooftop-solar financing barriers.

title: Integrating Energy Justice and SDGs in Solar Energy Transition: Analysis of the State Solar Policies of India
text:
Title: Integrating Energy Justice and SDGs in Solar Energy Transition: Analysis of the State Solar Policies of India
Authors: Bhavya Batra, Karina Standal, Solveig Aamodt, Gopal K. Sarangi & Manish Kumar Shrivastava (2025)
Journal / Source: Energies, 18(15), 3952 (2025), MDPI, DOI: 10.3390/en18153952 (Open Access, CC BY)
Objective: To assess whether India’s stated commitment to the SDG Agenda’s principle of "leaving no one behind" is reflected in the design of its state-level solar policies, using a purpose-built "Energy Justice–SDG Framework" (rooted in SDG 10) to evaluate income, inclusion and equal-opportunity dimensions across 29 state/UT solar policies.
Methodology: Qualitative interpretive content analysis (deductive coding) conducted in NVivo (v1.7.1); a novel "Energy Justice–SDG Framework" was first developed (3 dimensions derived from SDG 10 targets T10.1/T10.2/T10.3), then applied to code each policy document for the presence/absence of 15 justice indicators. No statistical or ML modeling — output is a frequency count of qualitative codes per state/UT.
Key Findings: (1) Financial instruments for developers are by far the most common justice mechanism (present in 25 of 29 policies), while gender-focused measures appear in only 3 states and targeted subsidies for small/marginal farmers in only 1 (Uttar Pradesh). (2) Only 4 states (Assam, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Uttarakhand) explicitly reference the SDGs in their policy vision/preamble. (3) Land-ownership-based inequalities are recognized in only 2 states (Goa, Kerala — via tribal/communidade land provisions). (4) Policies overwhelmingly favour "low-impact" justice concerns (energy access, employment, skilling) over structural/transformative justice (poverty reduction, gender equity, community ownership, land rights). (5) Community-owned/inclusive-governance provisions exist in only a handful of states (e.g., Jharkhand’s "model solar villages," Uttarakhand’s mandated women’s representation in village-level committees).
Limitations / Gaps: Confined to solar policy only (excludes wind, hydro, bioenergy, which may have different justice dynamics); analyzes policy DESIGN/text only, not implementation or on-the-ground outcomes; 4 states/UTs excluded for lack of an available or English-language policy (Nagaland, Tripura, Ladakh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra); the framework, while described as "pragmatic," covers only 51 of 169 SDG targets by the authors’ own inclusion criteria, so some relevant dimensions may be omitted; no primary stakeholder interviews to validate whether coded provisions are actually implemented or effective.
Future Work: Extend the Energy Justice–SDG Framework to other renewable sources (wind, hydro, bioenergy) and other Global-South countries; mixed-methods research combining the policy-text coding with field visits/stakeholder interviews to assess real-world implementation; incorporate quantitative household/regional adoption data to test whether states with stronger justice provisions show more equitable adoption outcomes (a natural complement to ML-based adoption-prediction studies).

title: Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission: A Critical Analysis of Evolution and Challenges
text:
Title: Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission: A Critical Analysis of Evolution and Challenges
Authors: Surya Prakash Upadhyay & Uttam Singh (2021)
Journal / Source: Book chapter in H. Tyagi et al. (Eds.), New Research Directions in Solar Energy Technologies (Energy, Environment, and Sustainability series), pp. 11–30, Springer Nature Singapore (2021), DOI: 10.1007/978-981-16-0594-9_2
Objective: To critically trace the evolution of the Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (JNNSM, launched Jan 2010) within the broader global climate-policy context (IPCC, UNFCCC, Kyoto, Rio, Cancun), analyze its phase-wise targets, financing and institutional architecture, and highlight the social/distributive challenges — solar e-waste, land use, and energy justice for marginalized communities — that the mission has not adequately addressed.
Methodology: Critical/interpretive policy analysis and literature synthesis; historical-institutional tracing of MNRE’s evolution (CASE 1981 → DNES 1982 → Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources 1992 → MNRE 2006); situates JNNSM within the international climate regime; draws on secondary case studies (Yenneti et al. 2016; Deshmukh et al. 2010) rather than original fieldwork or statistical/ML modeling.
Key Findings: (1) JNNSM’s target was revised upward twice (20 GW → 100 GW by 2015; split into 40 GW rooftop + 40 GW utility-scale + 20 GW via Ultra Mega Solar Parks) without a publicly transparent calculation methodology. (2) The mission is critiqued as a "non-participatory," market/political-mandate-driven process lacking meaningful public consultation (Deshmukh et al. 2010). (3) Off-grid/rural subsidy commitment is capped below 7% of total investment, disadvantaging poor and rural populations despite an "energy for all" framing. (4) Large solar parks (e.g., Charanka, Gujarat) generate positive regional/national benefits but negative local effects — better-off/upper-caste residents capture opportunities while poor and marginal farmers lose land and livelihoods (Yenneti et al. 2016). (5) No coherent national policy exists for solar-PV e-waste management, despite projected panel waste reaching ~2 million tonnes by 2030 (Bridge to India estimate). (6) Structural barriers persist: land availability for manufacturing, weak industry–government coordination, import dependency, low public awareness, multi-agency coordination delays (MNRE/SECI/IREDA/state boards), and skilled-manpower shortages.
Limitations / Gaps: Purely a secondary-source/desk-based critical review with no original fieldwork, interviews, or quantitative modeling; relies heavily on a narrow set of prior empirical studies (Deshmukh et al. 2010; Yenneti et al. 2016) for its key distributive-justice claims rather than independent verification; some cited figures (e.g., "4500 GW of renewable energy by 2030") appear inconsistently sourced; as a 2021 book chapter it does not capture post-2019 developments (2018 safeguard duty, PLI scheme); no discussion of ML/data-driven adoption-prediction approaches.
Future Work: Development of a coherent national e-waste/recycling policy framework for solar PV; deeper empirical (field-based) investigation of land-acquisition and community-participation processes across more solar parks beyond Charanka/Rewa; research into decentralized/community-owned models as alternatives to large Ultra Mega Solar Parks; stronger integration of energy-justice frameworks into mainstream techno-economic solar-mission evaluation.

title: Harnessing the Sun: India’s Legal and Policy Roadmap for Solar Energy
text:
Title: Harnessing the Sun: India’s Legal and Policy Roadmap for Solar Energy
Authors: Sanchit & Vanshika Sharma (2025)
Journal / Source: Working/student paper (SSRN Electronic Journal, SSRN id 5421475, 2025), Dr. B.R. Ambedkar National Law University, Sonepat — legal/policy analysis, not yet peer-reviewed in a journal
Objective: To provide a legal and policy analysis of India’s solar-energy sector — reviewing the National Solar Mission, Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPOs), Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs), the Electricity Act 2003, National Tariff Policy 2016, state-specific solar policies, and FDI/tax-incentive frameworks — and to identify legal/regulatory challenges and strategic opportunities for continued solar expansion.
Methodology: Doctrinal legal research / policy-review methodology — analysis of statutes, government policy documents and secondary commentary, structured thematically (legal framework → challenges → opportunities → recommendations); not empirical, statistical or ML-based.
Key Findings: (1) RPOs and RECs form the central compliance/market mechanism linking utility procurement obligations to renewable generation, letting resource-poor states meet obligations by purchasing RECs from resource-rich states. (2) The National Tariff Policy 2016’s "must-run" status for solar/wind is a key revenue-stability mechanism for developers. (3) 100% automatic-route FDI plus accelerated depreciation/tax exemptions have attracted large-scale investment, but high upfront capital costs remain a barrier, especially for rooftop and rural/economically weaker consumers. (4) Land acquisition and usage conflicts (agricultural vs. non-arable land, environmental clearances, community opposition) are a persistent bottleneck. (5) Grid-integration limitations stem from solar’s intermittency clashing with grid infrastructure built for conventional baseload sources. (6) State-level policy inconsistency (Gujarat vs. Rajasthan vs. Karnataka etc.) creates investor confusion; delayed RPO enforcement and inconsistent tariffs add financial risk. (7) Import dependence on PV cells/modules persists despite "Make in India" and the PLI scheme; skilled-workforce shortages remain, partly addressed via the Skill Council for Green Jobs (SCGJ).
Limitations / Gaps: Purely doctrinal/secondary-source based — no primary data collection, fieldwork, or quantitative/statistical modeling; relies substantially on non-peer-reviewed secondary media sources (LiveMint, PV Magazine India, ETEnergyworld, a blog) rather than peer-reviewed academic literature; does not quantify the relative impact of individual legal instruments; appears to be an unreviewed student/working paper (SSRN) rather than a peer-reviewed journal article; no discussion of ML/data-driven approaches.
Future Work: Empirical/quantitative evaluation of RPO compliance rates and REC market efficiency across states; comparative legal analysis of India’s solar regulatory framework against other major solar markets (China, USA, EU) to identify best-practice reforms; deeper legal analysis of land-acquisition dispute-resolution mechanisms specific to solar projects; assessment of the PLI scheme’s actual (not just intended) investment impact once more data becomes available.

title: Unleashing India’s Solar Potential: A Review of the National Solar Mission and the Path to Sustainable Energy in India
text:
Title: Unleashing India’s Solar Potential: A Review of the National Solar Mission and the Path to Sustainable Energy in India
Authors: Mubarak Musa Umar & Praveen Kumar Yadaw (2024)
Journal / Source: Journal of Technology Innovations and Energy, 3(2), 49–63 (2024), Global Scientific Research, ISSN 2957-8809, DOI: 10.56556/jtie.v3i2.930
Objective: To review India’s abundant solar-energy resources (availability, status, strategies, challenges, achievements and future prospects), with a specific focus on the JNNSM’s evolution and performance, and to project the sector’s future trajectory (market growth, state-wise grid-parity timelines, obstacles) to inform continued policy and investment support.
Methodology: Narrative/descriptive literature review combined with compiled secondary statistics and reproduced government/consultancy tables and figures (MNRE, CEA, KPMG, NSRDB); supplemented by unstructured "interviews with engineers, manufacturers, investors, regulators and legislators" (sample size/protocol undisclosed); no formal statistical or ML modeling — projections are stated as estimates without a disclosed quantitative model.
Key Findings: (1) JNNSM (launched Jan 11, 2010, targeting 22,000 MW) had, by August 2023, achieved 63,000 MW cumulative installed capacity — nearly 3× its original target — at ~18% average annual growth over the prior five years. (2) India’s total solar potential is estimated at ~750 GW, meaning current deployment represents a small fraction of the resource base. (3) State-level grid parity is projected earliest in Rajasthan and Gujarat (2017–2018, high irradiance and favourable policy) and latest in Bihar and West Bengal (2023–2024, lower initial investment/late adoption). (4) The sector moved from a "seed stage" (subsidy-driven, independent producers) into a "growth stage" (post-2016, driven by falling costs and grid-parity economics). (5) Obstacles fall into three categories: technological (DNI-data scarcity, assembly/infrastructure risk), policy/regulatory (inconsistent rules), and financial (land-title opacity, zoning complexity, easement-rights issues). (6) Developer success factors identified: "finalization" (execution speed/quality), financial support (concessional financing, e.g. Japan-linked joint ventures), and "local adaptation" (India-specific inverter/BOS engineering).
Limitations / Gaps: Significant sourcing/date inconsistencies throughout (e.g., citing "IEA 2024," "UN 2024," "IPCC 2024," "JNNSM 2024," "MNRE 2024" as generic access-dates for what are long-established historical facts; a figure captioned "Solar radiation of India" appears to actually show PV annual installation by region 2021–2027, suggesting a figure/caption mismatch); some claims read as internally inconsistent (e.g., a forward-looking ">50 GW by 2024" projection stated elsewhere alongside an already-achieved 63,000 MW/63 GW figure for Aug 2023); undisclosed interview methodology; published in a lower-visibility, limited-indexing journal; no original statistical or ML modeling; the state grid-parity table cites only a single secondary source (KPMG) without independent verification.
Future Work: Authors explicitly recommend: addressing grid-integration, storage and financing challenges as prerequisites for sustained growth; strengthening policy/regulatory frameworks and incentivizing private-sector participation; increasing R&D investment to harness the ~750 GW estimated potential; implicitly, more rigorous and consistently-sourced follow-on studies are needed given the sourcing issues within the review itself.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Section: Executive Summary

PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana has driven rooftop solar applications past 78 lakh nationally, yet the share of applications converted into completed installations varies dramatically across states — from 1.5% in Arunachal Pradesh to 92.9% in Mizoram. This variation is not well explained by subsidy amount or raw solar potential alone, a pattern consistent with prior literature (P2, P3). This report builds a verified 36-state panel from ten independently-sourced datasets, tests what actually predicts conversion efficiency, forecasts near-term national installation volume, and simulates two policy-relevant scenarios.

The central finding: a simple two-variable linear model — recent electricity tariff growth and long-run solar irradiance — explains 46% of in-sample variation in state-level conversion ratio and generalizes better (Leave-One-Out cross-validated MAE 0.135) than a six-feature Random Forest (MAE 0.161). Subsidy/tariff level and raw solar potential are consistently the weakest predictors across every method tested. This is direct evidence that adoption efficiency is driven more by economic momentum and physical resource fit than by subsidy generosity itself.

title: 1. Introduction and Problem Statement
text:
Section: 1. Introduction and Problem Statement

PM Surya Ghar, launched in February 2024 with an outlay exceeding ₹75,000 crore, aims to subsidize rooftop solar installation for one crore households. While national application volumes have grown steadily, prior research (P2, P3) found that the share of applications converted into completed installations is not well explained by subsidy levels alone, varying from 1.15% to 85.91% across states. This project treats PM Surya Ghar as a data science and policy analytics problem: building a clean state-level panel, identifying what actually predicts adoption efficiency, and testing policy-relevant scenarios.

title: 1.1 Research Questions
text:
Section: 1.1 Research Questions

Which states convert applications into installations most/least efficiently, and why?

Do administrative and physical-resource variables outperform subsidy amount as predictors of conversion efficiency?

Can near-term national installation volume be forecast from available historical data?

What would a tariff increase, or targeting high-potential/low-adoption states, be expected to yield under current model assumptions?

title: 1.2 Contribution and Scope
text:
Section: 1.2 Contribution and Scope

This work reproduces the subsidy-paradox finding from prior literature using more recent data (conversion ratio range 1.5%–92.9%, wider than the 1.15%–85.91% previously reported), and takes a first step toward explaining it. It does not claim to be the first application of machine learning to Indian solar energy — ML is already used in generation forecasting — nor does it claim to discover the subsidy paradox, which prior work identified. Its contribution is a rigorously verified panel, an honest small-sample model comparison, and transparent documentation of what remains unresolved.

title: 2.1 Datasets Collected
text:
Section: 2.1 Datasets Collected

Ten datasets were individually sourced, cross-verified against official totals, and merged into a canonical 36-state panel. Each dataset's totals were checked against at least one independent source before inclusion (e.g., the PMSG portal dashboard, Rajya Sabha replies, or the source PDF the figure was extracted from).

title: 2.2 Deliberately Excluded Datasets
text:
Section: 2.2 Deliberately Excluded Datasets

Two datasets from the original Tier 1 list were scoped out rather than force-collected:

Net-metering regime — no centralized source exists; would require 28 separate state regulatory-commission lookups.

State-level subsidy top-up — no centralized source; budgets vary by state and are time-limited, adding a dating problem on top of the access problem.

Both exclusions are treated as documented limitations, not silent gaps — Section 6 discusses their implications for the scenario analysis.

title: 2.3 Panel Construction and Target Variable
text:
Section: 2.3 Panel Construction and Target Variable

State names were normalized against a canonical 36-state/UT list; Urban/Rural tariff splits were averaged into single state-level figures; DISCOM-specific rows (e.g., Torrent Power, Mumbai BEST/Adani/TATA) were excluded from state totals to avoid double-counting. One transcription error ("Telengana" for "Telangana" in the irradiance source) was caught during this process and corrected.

The target variable — installations ÷ applications, hereafter conversion ratio — was chosen over raw installation counts for three reasons: it is scale-free (comparable across states of very different size without population data), it is central to the literature's subsidy-paradox framing, and the available scheme-progress snapshots are too sparse and irregularly dated (10+ weeks apart in places) to support a clean levels-based time series.

title: 3. Exploratory Findings
text:
Section: 3. Exploratory Findings

Conversion ratio across 35 states with complete data ranges from 1.5% (Arunachal Pradesh) to 92.9% (Mizoram) as of the 23 August 2026 snapshot.

Figure 1. Application-to-installation conversion ratio by state.

Correlating conversion ratio against every collected covariate found two variables with a meaningfully non-zero relationship: 2024→2025 tariff growth (r = +0.53, n = 34) and solar irradiance (r = +0.51, n = 28). Subsidy/tariff level, raw solar potential, and application volume itself showed near-zero correlation (|r| < 0.15) across the board.

Figure 2. Irradiance and tariff-growth scatter plots against conversion ratio.

title: 4. Predictive Modeling
text:
Section: 4. Predictive Modeling

Two model families were compared using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation, appropriate given the small sample size (28–35 states).

The simple two-feature linear model outperformed the six-feature Random Forest — with only 28 rows, additional features caused overfitting rather than improved generalization. This finding was cross-checked with SHAP values on the Random Forest model; tariff growth and irradiance ranked highest by both Gini importance and mean |SHAP value|, agreeing with the linear model's coefficients.

Figure 3. SHAP summary plot — feature impact on the Random Forest's predictions.

Best-fit equation: Conversion Ratio ≈ –0.707 + 1.607 × (tariff growth %) + 0.250 × (irradiance, kWh/m²/day). In-sample R² = 0.455; this is reported for reference only and is not equivalent to predictive power — the LOO-CV MAE above is the honest generalization estimate.

title: 5. Forecasting
text:
Section: 5. Forecasting

National cumulative installations were forecast from six dated official releases spanning November 2024 to August 2026 — eighteen months since scheme launch. This is too few points to safely fit ARIMA or SARIMAX without overfitting, so naive, linear, and log-linear (exponential growth) extrapolation were compared by in-sample MAPE.

Log-linear extrapolation fit substantially better, consistent with a subsidy scheme still in its ramp-up phase. Forecasts with 95% prediction intervals:

Figure 4. Observed installations and log-linear forecast with 95% prediction interval.

This forecast assumes the current growth rate continues; real-world adoption typically follows an S-curve that eventually flattens as the addressable market saturates. The 12-month forecast should be treated with more caution than the 3-month forecast for this reason.

title: 6. Scenario Analysis
text:
Section: 6. Scenario Analysis

The guideline defines five scenarios (A–E). Only three are genuinely supportable given the model's two features (tariff growth, irradiance) — Scenario B (subsidy +10%) and the subsidy component of Scenario E cannot be simulated, since state-level subsidy data was not collected (Section 2.2). This is stated explicitly rather than fabricated.

title: 6.1 Scenario C — High Solar Potential Targeting
text:
Section: 6.1 Scenario C — High Solar Potential Targeting

States with above-median irradiance but below-median conversion ratio — a direct "high-potential, low-adoption" profile — are: Gujarat, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh, and Andhra Pradesh. These are reasonable candidates for differentiated policy attention, since physical solar resource is not their binding constraint.

title: 6.2 Scenario D — Tariff Increase
text:
Section: 6.2 Scenario D — Tariff Increase

Simulating a +10 percentage-point tariff-growth shock predicts a uniform +16 percentage-point lift in conversion ratio for every state.

Figure 5. Predicted mean conversion-ratio lift under tariff growth shocks.

This uniformity is a modeling limitation, not necessarily a real-world finding: the linear model has no interaction terms, so it cannot express that a state near adoption saturation might respond less than a state with more headroom. A model with tariff × current-adoption interaction terms is a natural next step, not attempted here given the sample size.

title: 6.3 Scenario E — Combined Intervention (Partial)
text:
Section: 6.3 Scenario E — Combined Intervention (Partial)

The tariff-shock component of Scenario D was applied specifically to the four Scenario C targeting states, yielding the same uniform +16pp lift. The subsidy-increase component that would complete this scenario is not modeled.

title: 7. Limitations
text:
Section: 7. Limitations

Small sample size: 28–35 states is limited for a six-feature model; the Random Forest result should be read as a caution against overfitting, not a strong finding in its own right.

Cross-sectional, not longitudinal: all modeling uses a single dated snapshot (23 August 2026). Whether the tariff-growth/irradiance relationship holds requires a second aligned cross-section at a future date.

Correlational, not causal: none of the reported relationships should be interpreted causally without a proper identification strategy (difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, or synthetic control), none of which was attempted here.

Limited historical depth: PM Surya Ghar launched in February 2024; only six dated national installation figures exist across eighteen months, constraining the forecasting methodology to simple extrapolation.

Missing subsidy and net-metering data: two Tier 1 datasets were deliberately not collected due to the absence of a centralized source, limiting Scenario B and part of Scenario E.

Source disagreement: official releases occasionally disagree on the same metric for close dates (e.g., a household count differing by roughly 38,000 between two releases one day apart in early August 2026) — the more granular, traceable source was preferred in each case, and the discrepancy is logged rather than silently resolved.

No population normalization: state population data was not collected, so per-capita installation rates are not reported here.

title: 8. Conclusion and Future Work
text:
Section: 8. Conclusion and Future Work

This project set out to explain why PM Surya Ghar conversion efficiency varies so widely across Indian states. The strongest, most consistent finding across correlation analysis, linear regression, Random Forest importance, and SHAP values is that tariff growth and solar irradiance predict conversion efficiency meaningfully better than subsidy level or raw solar potential — direct evidence against a "subsidy amount alone" explanation, and a concrete first step toward resolving the subsidy paradox identified in prior literature.

Future work should prioritize, in order: (1) collecting state-level subsidy top-up data to properly test Scenario B; (2) obtaining a second aligned cross-section to test whether the tariff-growth/irradiance relationship is stable over time, which would meaningfully strengthen the causal plausibility of these findings; (3) adding interaction terms to the model to capture state-specific responsiveness to tariff changes; and (4) sourcing state population data to enable per-capita normalized analysis.
